body.statement: Derive an explicit rate \(r_n(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,d)\), including every phase boundary and every necessary equality-case logarithm, and prove \(c_{\mathrm{rate}}r_n\le\rho_\star(n)\le C_{\mathrm{rate}}r_n\) over the observed image \(\mathcal P^{\mathrm{obs}}\) for every \(n\ge n_0\). The upper inequality must be attained by a total data-computable test with uniform size and power; the lower inequality must hold for all randomized tests via priors on observed laws in \(\mathcal P^{\mathrm{obs}}\) whose full-law null lifts each have constant \(\tau^{\mathrm F}\) and exact uniform design. Determine from the derived formula whether \(r_n=r_{\mathrm{or}}\), and exactly where learning \(e\) and \(\mu_0\) changes the benchmark; \(R_{\mathrm{up}}\) is one candidate upper bound and is not prescribed as the answer.
body.justification: The same-class converse is the theorem-level kernel; it decides whether rough confounding genuinely alters omnibus detectability rather than merely degrading a particular estimator.
body.gap: KennedyBalakrishnanRobinsWasserman2024 proves a nuisance elbow for pointwise CATE estimation, while KotekalKundu2025 proves a rough-mean elbow for heteroskedasticity testing; neither supplies constant-CATE testing priors that preserve this model's baseline smoothness and exact uniform design.
body.consumer: A sharp answer identifies when dScoreTest's first-order hunting route can be omnibus-rate optimal and when a higher-order calibrated alternative is statistically necessary.
